assignment.title: Rational Exponents
assignment.essentialQuestion: Why can it be useful to simplify expressions?
assignment.teacherNotes: Bluebonnet Algebra II — Radicals, Lesson 3 (Rational Exponents), TEKS A2.7G. Answers are graded in the notation the key uses: a “radical form” key needs a radical and an “exponential form” key a rational exponent; simplified means positive exponents, no fractional exponent in a denominator, reduced exponents and the smallest index. Exact values are required where asked — a calculator decimal for 1/7 is marked not yet. Warm-Up and DOL are generated per student and back Recovery.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt{ {{R}} a^3 }$.
hints: Find the largest perfect square that divides {{R}}, and split a³ into a² · a.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. √(a³) simplifies to…

solutionReview.headline: Take out the largest perfect square.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving a² under the radical: a² is a perfect square and comes out as a.

questions.prompt: Rationalize the denominator: $\dfrac{ {{c}} }{ \sqrt{ {{k}} } }$.
hints: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by √{{k}}.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For a positive number k, what is √k · √k?

solutionReview.headline: Multiply the top and the bottom by √{{k}}.
reasoning: The denominator √{{k}} · √{{k}} = {{k}} has no radical left.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying only the denominator by √{{k}} changes the value of the fraction.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (u + v)(u − v) equals…

solutionReview.headline: A sum times a difference is a difference of squares.

questions.prompt: Properties of exponents. Simplify each expression; write answers with positive exponents only. Assume no variable equals 0. $\;(a^{-3})(a^2b^4)(c^{-1})$, $\;\dfrac{n^2}{n^{10}}$, $\;\left(\dfrac{3a^3}{b^4}\right)^2$

steps.title: Product and quotient of powers
steps.instruction: aᵐ · aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (a ≠ 0).

steps.title: Simplified monomial
steps.instruction: No powers of powers, each base appears once, all fractions in lowest terms, no negative exponents.

hints: Add the exponents of the same base; a negative exponent moves its factor to the denominator.
Subtract exponents when dividing powers of the same base, then rewrite a negative exponent.
Square the 3, the a³ and the b⁴.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What does a⁻¹ mean?

solutionReview.headline: Use the properties of exponents, then clear negative exponents.
solutionReview.commonError: A negative exponent makes a reciprocal, not a negative number: a⁻¹ is 1/a.

questions.prompt: The definition $b^{\frac{1}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{b}$. Rewrite and evaluate each.

steps.title: Rational exponent 1/n
steps.instruction: For a real number b and an integer n > 1, b^(1/n) = ⁿ√b, when ⁿ√b is real.

steps.title: Even roots of negatives
steps.instruction: An even root of a negative number is not real: (−16)^(1/2) = √(−16) = 4i.

hints: The denominator of the exponent is the index of the root.
A square root has index 2.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In b^(1/n), what does n tell you?

solutionReview.headline: b^(1/n) is the nth root of b.
reasoning: (−16)^(1/2) = √(−16), an even root of a negative number: it is not a real number (it is 4i).
solutionReview.answerSummary: ⁷√a; w^(1/2); 3; not a real number

questions.prompt: Evaluate $49^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ and $32^{\frac{2}{5}}$. Show the root first.

steps.title: Rational exponent m/n
steps.instruction: b^(m/n) = (ⁿ√b)ᵐ = ⁿ√(bᵐ). Taking the root first keeps the numbers small: 32^(2/5) = (⁵√32)² = 2² = 4.

hints: ⁵√32 asks: which number to the fifth power is 32?

misconceptions.message: A negative exponent makes a reciprocal, not a negative number: 49^(−1/2) = 1/49^(1/2).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What does a negative exponent do?

solutionReview.headline: Take the root first.
solutionReview.commonError: 49^(−1/2) is 1/7, not −7: the negative exponent makes a reciprocal.

questions.prompt: Evaluate exactly (no decimals): $25^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, $16^{\frac{3}{4}}$ and $27^{\frac{2}{3}}$.
hints: Take the root first: the denominator of the exponent is the index.
Then raise the root to the power in the numerator; a negative exponent makes a reciprocal.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In 16^(3/4), what do you do first to keep the numbers small?

solutionReview.headline: Root first, then the power.
solutionReview.commonError: 16^(3/4) is not 16 · 3/4 = 12: a rational exponent is a root and a power.

questions.prompt: Weightlifting. The formula $M = 512 - 146{,}230B^{-\frac{8}{5}}$ estimates the maximum total mass $M$ (kg) that a weightlifter of mass $B$ kilograms can lift in the snatch and the clean and jerk combined. What does it predict for a lifter of mass 168 kg, to the nearest kilogram?
hints: Evaluate 168^(−8/5) first: it is 1/168^(8/5).
Multiply that by 146,230, subtract the product from 512, and round to the nearest kilogram.

solutionReview.headline: Substitute and evaluate the rational power.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. B^(−8/5) is the same as…

questions.prompt: Simplify each expression; leave no negative exponents and no fractional exponent in a denominator. $\;y^{\frac{1}{7}} \cdot y^{\frac{4}{7}}$ and $\;x^{-\frac{2}{3}}$

steps.title: Simplified form with rational exponents
steps.instruction: No negative exponents; no fractional exponents in the denominator; not a complex fraction; the index of any remaining radical is as small as possible.

steps.title: Clearing a fractional exponent from a denominator

hints: Add exponents when multiplying powers with the same base.
For x^(−2/3) = 1/x^(2/3), multiply the top and the bottom by the power of x that brings x^(2/3) up to x¹.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. When you multiply powers with the same base, what do you do with the exponents?

solutionReview.headline: Add exponents; then clear the denominator.
solutionReview.commonError: 1/x^(2/3) still has a fractional exponent in the denominator, so it is not simplified.

questions.prompt: Use rational exponents to simplify $\dfrac{\sqrt[6]{16}}{\sqrt[3]{2}}$ and $\sqrt[6]{4x^4}$.
hints: Write 16 as a power of 2, write the sixth root as the exponent 1/6, and reduce.
Write the cube root as a power of 2 too; dividing powers of the same base subtracts the exponents.
Write 4x⁴ as 2²x⁴, raise it to the power 1/6, and reduce each exponent.

solutionReview.headline: Rewrite with rational exponents, simplify, return to radicals.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving ⁶√(4x⁴): the index 6 is not the smallest possible.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. How is ⁶√16 written with a rational exponent?

questions.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{y^{\frac{1}{2}} + 1}{y^{\frac{1}{2}} - 1}$ so that no fractional exponent is left in the denominator.

responses.label: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by

hints: Multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
The product of conjugates (a − b)(a + b) is a² − b², and (y^(1/2))² = y.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is the conjugate of a − b?

solutionReview.headline: Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator.
reasoning: Multiply the top and the bottom by y^(1/2) + 1.
solutionReview.commonError: (y^(1/2) + 1)² is not y + 1: the middle term 2y^(1/2) is easy to drop.

questions.prompt: Sort each expression: simplified, or not yet simplified? Use the rules for rational exponents and radicals.
hints: A negative exponent, a fractional exponent in a denominator, an unreduced exponent, a larger-than-needed index, or a base written twice means not yet.

solutionReview.headline: Check every rule for simplified form.
reasoning: Not yet: x^(−2/3) has a negative exponent (it is x^(1/3)/x); 1/x^(1/2) has a fractional exponent in the denominator (x^(1/2)/x); y^(10/14) reduces to y^(5/7); ⁶√(4x⁴) has a larger index than needed (∛(2x²)); y^(1/7) · y^(4/7) writes the base twice (y^(5/7)).
solutionReview.commonError: x^(1/3)/x is simplified: the denominator x has a whole-number exponent.

questions.prompt: Simplify; positive exponents only. Assume no variable equals 0. $\;(x^{-2}y^{-3})(x^{-3}y^5)(z^2)$, $\;\dfrac{h^6}{h^{-2}}$, $\;\left(\dfrac{6r^2}{3s^3}\right)^2$
hints: Collect each base and add its exponents; then move negative exponents to the denominator.
Dividing by h⁻² is multiplying by h².
Simplify 6/3 first.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. h⁶/h⁻² means you…

solutionReview.headline: Collect each base, then clear negative exponents.
reasoning: x⁻²x⁻³ = x⁻⁵ and y⁻³y⁵ = y², so (x⁻²y⁻³)(x⁻³y⁵)(z²) = y²z²/x⁵.
solutionReview.commonError: h⁶/h⁻² is not h⁴: subtracting a negative exponent adds.

questions.prompt: Simplify: $x^{\frac{ {{a}} }{ {{n}} }} \cdot x^{\frac{ {{b}} }{ {{n}} }}$
hints: Add the exponents.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Multiplying powers with the same base, you…

solutionReview.headline: Add the exponents.
reasoning: {{n}} is prime and {{s}} < {{n}}, so the exponent is already in lowest terms.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying the exponents gives a power of x that is much too small.

questions.prompt: Rewrite each expression in the other form.
hints: b^(m/n) = ⁿ√(bᵐ): the denominator is the index.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In b^(m/n) = ⁿ√(bᵐ), which number is the index?

solutionReview.headline: The denominator of the exponent is the index; the numerator is the power.
solutionReview.commonError: ∛(x²) is x^(2/3), not x^(3/2): the index goes in the denominator.

questions.prompt: Evaluate exactly: ${{b}}^{\frac{ {{m}} }{ {{n}} }}$. Show the root first.
hints: In b^(m/n), the denominator n names the root and the numerator m the power: b^(m/n) = (ⁿ√b)^m.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In b^(m/n), which part names the root?

solutionReview.headline: Root first, then the power.
reasoning: Raise that root to the power {{m}}: {{b}}^({{m}}/{{n}}) = {{v}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying {{b}} by {{m}}/{{n}} is not a rational exponent: it means a root and a power.

questions.prompt: Evaluate exactly: ${{b}}^{-\frac{ {{m}} }{ {{n}} }}$
hints: A negative exponent means the reciprocal: 1/{{b}}^({{m}}/{{n}}).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A negative exponent tells you to…

solutionReview.headline: A negative exponent makes a reciprocal.
solutionReview.commonError: −{{v}} is not the value: the negative exponent makes a reciprocal, not a negative number.

questions.prompt: Simplify: $x^{\frac{1}{5}} \cdot x^{\frac{2}{5}}$ and $y^{-\frac{3}{4}}$.
hints: A negative exponent means a reciprocal: y^(−3/4) = 1/y^(3/4). Then clear the fractional exponent from the denominator.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is y^(3/4) · y^(1/4)?

solutionReview.headline: Add exponents; then clear the denominator.
solutionReview.commonError: 1/y^(3/4) still has a fractional exponent in the denominator.

questions.prompt: Simplify: $\dfrac{\sqrt[4]{4}}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\sqrt[6]{16x^2}$. Assume $x > 0$.
hints: Write 4 as a power of 2 and the fourth root as the exponent 1/4.
Write 16x² as 2⁴x², raise it to the power 1/6, and reduce each exponent.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is 4 as a power of 2?

solutionReview.headline: Write each radical with a rational exponent and reduce.
solutionReview.commonError: Reducing ⁶√(16x²) to ∛(16x) divides only the exponent of x: 16 = 2⁴ must be reduced too.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{x^{\frac{1}{2}} - 1}{x^{\frac{1}{2}} + 1}$ so that no fractional exponent is left in the denominator.
hints: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by x^(1/2) − 1.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (x^(1/2) + 1)(x^(1/2) − 1) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator.
reasoning: Multiply the top and the bottom by x^(1/2) − 1.
solutionReview.commonError: (x^(1/2) − 1)² is not x − 1: it has the middle term −2x^(1/2).

questions.prompt: Use $M = 512 - 146{,}230B^{-\frac{8}{5}}$, where $M$ is the maximum total mass (kg) a weightlifter of mass $B$ kilograms can lift. What does the formula predict for a lifter of mass 80 kg, to the nearest kilogram?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which number do you substitute for B?

solutionReview.headline: Substitute B = 80 and evaluate in order.

questions.prompt: The equation $y = 10m^{\frac{3}{4}}$ estimates the energy output $y$ (kcal/day) of a reptile with body mass $m$ kilograms. An average alligator has a mass of 360 kilograms. Estimate its energy output to the nearest tenth.
hints: Find 360^(3/4) as (⁴√360)³, then multiply by 10.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What value of m do you substitute?

solutionReview.headline: Substitute m = 360, then root, power and multiply.
solutionReview.commonError: 360^(3/4) is not 360 × 3/4 = 270: the exponent means a fourth root and a cube.

questions.prompt: Simplify: $(8x^6)^{-\frac{2}{3}}$ and $\sqrt[4]{36}$.
hints: Apply the power to each factor, (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ, then rewrite the negative exponent.
Write 36 as a power of 6 and reduce the exponent.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In (8x⁶)^(−2/3), which factors are raised to the power −2/3?

solutionReview.headline: Apply the exponent to each factor; reduce.
solutionReview.commonError: Applying −2/3 only to x⁶ leaves 8 unchanged, but the exponent applies to both factors.

questions.prompt: Sort each expression: simplified, or not yet simplified?
hints: Check each rule: no negative exponents, no fractional exponent in a denominator, reduced exponents, the smallest index.

solutionReview.headline: Check every rule for simplified form.
reasoning: Not yet: a^(4/10) reduces to a^(2/5); b^(−1/2) has a negative exponent (b^(1/2)/b); 1/c^(3/4) has a fractional exponent in the denominator (c^(1/4)/c); ⁴√25 = √5 has a smaller index.
solutionReview.commonError: b^(1/2)/b is simplified: the fractional exponent is in the numerator.

questions.prompt: Evaluate exactly: ${{b}}^{\frac{ {{m}} }{ {{n}} }}$. Show the root first.

solutionReview.headline: Root first, then the power.
reasoning: Raise that root to the power {{m}}: {{b}}^({{m}}/{{n}}) = {{v}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying {{b}} by {{m}}/{{n}} is not a rational exponent: it means a root and a power.

questions.prompt: Simplify; leave no negative exponent and no fractional exponent in a denominator: ${{k|coef}}x^{-\frac{ {{a}} }{ {{n}} }}$

solutionReview.headline: Rewrite the negative exponent, then clear the denominator.
reasoning: Multiply the top and the bottom by x^({{b}}/{{n}}): x^({{a}}/{{n}}) · x^({{b}}/{{n}}) = x.
solutionReview.commonError: {{k}}/x^({{a}}/{{n}}) still has a fractional exponent in the denominator.
